Business.title: Drivers may get compensation offers before car finance saga ends
Business.text:
Drivers may be offered compensation from lenders ahead of the next legal battle in the car finance mis-selling saga.

Regulator the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said it would welcome lenders making settlement offers as long as customers were not given a worse deal than under its proposed central scheme.

That scheme is facing a legal challenge, to be heard in February, with resulting compensation unlikely to be paid until late next year.

But Barclays has confirmed it will make early compensation offers from now, with others expected to follow suit.

The FCA said it would still only expect a minority of claimants to be made early offers, with most having to wait for the outcome of next year's court case.

Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA's general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said: "Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. It's clear they want the choice.

"Anyone who wants to wait can, and there's no obligation to agree to the offer. We'll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means."

The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest.

But millions of drivers who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024 will be entitled to compensation after the loans were mis-sold.

They mostly related to when car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them.

Average compensation payouts of about £829 are expected to be made related to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period.

Compensation will cost the industry up to £9.1bn, including administrative costs. Individual payouts will vary, depending on the degree of harm each driver faced.

With huge compensation payouts inevitable, some lenders have already set aside millions of pounds to cover the cost.

Barclays has decided to start making compensation payments early, potentially to start clearing the cost off its balance sheet. It pointed out that claimants had already faced "a considerable wait".

"By making these early settlement offers, we are giving some customers the option of receiving redress sooner, rather than waiting for the legal challenges and any subsequent FCA action to conclude," said a Barclays Partner Finance spokesperson.

"Each offer will be calculated using the FCA's redress scheme methodology. We will clearly explain how it has been calculated and what accepting a full and final settlement means, so customers can decide whether accepting the offer is right for them."

The lender said claimants would start to be contacted directly "in the coming weeks".

But it stressed not all customers whose complaints were acknowledged on or before 1 October 2026 would receive an early settlement offer.

The FCA has published a factsheet to help drivers, external work out whether they should accept early settlements from lenders.

It will include a list of lenders who are making early offers, to ensure claimants with other lenders are not scammed.

The regulator said lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes:

Being able to keep any payment, even if the final settlement under the central scheme after the legal challenges proved to be smaller

Claimants would not be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge meant they would have been paid more

Accepting an offer takes you out of the scheme and stops any further input from the financial ombudsman

The Finance and Leasing Association, which represents lenders, said: "We want to see consumers receive the fairest outcome in as timely a way as possible and recognise that, in some cases, that may point to early settlement, while in others it may be appropriate to await greater legal certainty."

But Kevin Durkin, solicitor advocate and director at HD Law, who represented Marcus Johnson who won his case in the Supreme Court, said he had "real reservations" that fair compensation would be offered.

"These are only heightened by reports that just a small number of claimants will receive what could be lowball offers. I fear this is crumbs from the table, for some customers who are highly likely to be owed more, while the vast majority will receive no offer at all," he said.

The main proposed FCA scheme remains partially suspended, pending legal challenges in February.

Consumer group Consumer Voice said the proposed compensation scheme left "too many people short-changed". Three lenders - Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance - are also challenging the scheme.

The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled from 16 February to 3 March.

Anyone who is concerned about their car finance deal and has not yet complained can still complain directly to their lender. There is information on the FCA website on how to complain for free, external.

Business.title: Asda hires former Morrisons boss David Potts in bid to grow firm
Business.text:
Asda has appointed a former Morrisons boss as chief executive to help lead revival efforts at the supermarket chain.

Asda, which is based in Leeds, said David Potts would take on the role with immediate effect, while current boss Allan Leighton would become non-executive chairman, two years after returning to lead the supermarket chain.

Potts led Morrisons from its Bradford headquarters for eight years until 2023, overseeing a turnaround during which the supermarket chain was bought by US private equity firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice.

Potts said Asda had "made good progress but significant opportunities remain" to reinvigorate sales, with a focus on keeping prices low for shoppers.

"By making improvements to the shopping trip every week, which customers can experience and feel in their pockets, we will revitalise the business and bring benefits for all our stakeholders, including our 116,296 very hard-working colleagues," he said.

Before joining Morrisons, Potts was chief executive of Tesco's Irish business, its UK arm and its Asian operation.

According to Asda, Leighton had planned to step aside from the day-to-day running of the group, after he returned in 2024, more than two decades after serving as chief executive.

"Over the last two years, we have stabilised the business and returned it to some growth," said Leighton.

"David has an outstanding record in our industry, his experience is exactly what we now require for the next stage of our transformation and beyond and it will be great to work with him."

Last year, issues with an IT upgrade hit product availability at the supermarket and dented sales, impacting its bottom line.

But in August, it reported sales had returned to growth for the current quarter for the first time in two years.

Business.title: Rio Tinto joins fight to stop killer toad march across Australia
Business.text:
Rio Tinto is ploughing millions of dollars into stopping the poisonous cane toad reaching the Pilbara region of western Australia, where the mining giant has a vast iron ore operation.

The firm, alongside Curtin University in Perth and others, will spend A$28m (£14.5m) building a "toad containment zone" to prevent the pest travelling south.

While the cane toad is not a direct threat to Rio Tinto's business, it produces toxins lethal to native wildlife and poses a threat to Pilbara's ecosystem.

Rio Tinto has previously faced criticism for destroying two sacred Aboriginal rock shelters in Pilbara which sat above tonnes of iron ore.

The decision cost the former chief executive his job, provoked a widespread backlash and saw Rio Tinto commit to rebuilding trust with Indigenous communities.

Commenting on the proposed containment zone, Roberta Hunter, a ranger in Australia's Nyangumarta Warrarn Indigenous Protected Area, said: "Cane toads destroy the water and animals.

"When toads come close to our country, we want to be there to stop them because we don't want the country to be destroyed."

The plan is to cut off the toad's water supply by building a barrier across 7,500 sq km (2,895 sq m) of land between the Great Sandy Desert and the Indian Ocean.

In drier months, the cane toad needs water every few days to survive.

If there are no natural water sources, the toad relies on artificial water points normally used for cattle and irrigation.

The funding will be used to stop the toad accessing dams, storage tanks or other ground-level water sources. The five-year project will begin in 2027.

A number of native species are at risk if the toad gets into Pilbara. These include the northern quoll, whose numbers have been decreasing, the goanna lizard and the ghost bat.

The toads were introduced into Australia in 1935 to control beetles within the sugar cane industry.

Business.title: From scooters to shampoo - the people saving hundreds from dumpster diving
Business.text:
Darryl Baker was shocked to see piles of clothes dumped beside the recycling bins outside her local supermarket.

On several trips to the dumpsters she has also found a host of other items, such as "a perfectly decent" Ikea picture frame and children's scooters.

Always on the lookout for ways to save money and appalled by the waste, the thrifty mother-of-two from north London asked supermarket staff if she could take some of it.

Permission granted, "I got my children entire new wardrobes," says Darryl, 39, adding that she's stuff put away for years to come.

During a six-month stint this year, "I have probably saved hundreds of pounds," says the freelance journalist.

Darryl reels off the names of brands she has salvaged - Ralph Lauren, Nike and The North Face, among others. "My mind was blown," she says. "This stuff is just strewn all over the floor."

Texan Jeff Ferrell has been rooting around in trash for more than 50 years.

"I still dumpster dive every day by bicycle," says the 72-year old, who lives in Fort Worth, and has written books on the topic. "I still enjoy it as much, or more, than ever."

Jeff considers himself a "bit of Robin Hood mixed with anarchist direct action", only scrounging in more affluent neighbourhoods and giving away many of his finds.

"Almost everything in our home is scrounged, and I never buy, for example, soap or toiletries or medical supplies, or shoes and clothes and tools and garden supplies," he says.

She estimates that one dress she found was worth £600.

"I'm a bit of a magpie. I like collecting things off the street or anywhere that there's a freebie. If I see something that catches my eye, then I'll grab it."

Millie, 36, began bin diving after spotting some fabrics discarded by a business that had shut down. "I literally clambered into the bin. It turned out it was loads of vintage clothes."

But is taking things out of bins and keeping them acceptable in the eyes of the law?

Jeff, who is professor emeritus of sociology at Texas Christian University, says many US cities have made the practice illegal, including New York, Cleveland and Wichita.

"Dumpster diving is considered illegal [in such places] because that which is thrown away now belongs to the city... or to the private company that provided trash services," he explains. Any dumpster diver also risks trespass charges.

In Fort Worth, where Jeff lives, items can only be removed from bins if they are on public land, external.

In the UK, Sunjay Versani of Duncan Lewis Solicitors says it depends on the circumstances.

"In many cases involving genuinely discarded goods, prosecution is unlikely," he says.

"But there is no general rule that something is free to take simply because it has been put in a skip or bin. If in doubt, the safest approach is to ask the owner or business for permission."

Business.title: 'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why
Business.text:
The so-called "quiet quitting" trend where workers do the basic requirements of a job but refuse to do anything more might be hitting the economy, analysis has found.

Over the last decade, Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, according to a Resolution Foundation report.

The thinktank said this could partly help explain the slump in productivity since the pandemic.

"This is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn't bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead," said Hannah Slaughter, principal economist at the Resolution Foundation.

Quiet quitting was popularised on social media shortly after the pandemic.

Frustrated by high demands, low pay, and a squeeze in living standards, many online posts said workers should only do what their bosses asked and nothing more.

So you still show up for work, but no more helping out with additional tasks or checking emails outside work hours, instead focusing on work-life balance and "acting your wage".

Yet, far from being just a talking point on TikTok, the Resolution Foundation said the findings in its report were "consistent" with the idea of quiet quitting.

The percentage of those surveyed willing to go the extra mile to help their employer has sunk from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025, according to their survey of 4,656 adults.

Meanwhile, those who were not even "fairly" satisfied with their roles has sunk to one-in-four, the lowest level on record.

In addition, workers are less likely than 10 years ago to say they have an interesting job, with 63% of those surveyed saying so, down from 74%.

"Workers today are indeed a little less committed to their employers, and a little less intrinsically drawn to work in general, than workers were a decade ago," the report added.

This shift over the last decade "may have contributed to weak productivity growth", which has slowed since the financial crisis and weakened again after the pandemic, the Resolution Foundation found.

Workers were also more focused on pay than in the past, which it said was "perhaps unsurprising... given the flatlining living standards of the past decade".

Sir John Curtice, politics professor and co-editor of the report, said the analysis does not mean that young people have "become more 'work-shy', nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs".

"But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financially rewarding and have flexible work hours," he added.

Business.title: USA Olympic and Paralympic Committee could seek private investment for commercial rights
Business.text:
The United States Olympic and Paralympic Committee (USOPC) could sell a stake in commercial rights for Team USA to private investors.

In a statement, the USOPC said it is "evaluating a range of commercial models to generate greater resources in support of its mission".

They involve the establishment of a new company called United States Olympic and Paralympic Ventures (USOPV).

It comes as the US prepares to host both the Los Angeles Summer Games in 2028 and 2034 Winter Games in Utah.

USOPC currently has a commercial partnership with the LA 2028 Organising Committee as part of a deal that will expire after the Games.

But as first reported by Sky News and Reuters, the organisation has been in talks about various options.

According to USOPC board minutes, it has had "encouraging feedback from preliminary discussions with potential investment and strategic partners [who] generally validated the vision for the USOPV and strategic rationale underlying the initiative".

In a statement, USOPC, a non-profit organisation, said: "The next decade represents an unprecedented opportunity for Team USA and the US Olympic and Paralympic Movement.

"As part of our responsibility to maximise that opportunity for the athletes and NGBs (national governing bodies) we serve, the USOPC is evaluating a range of commercial models to generate greater resources in support of its mission.

"We've been in ongoing conversation with athlete and NGB leaders during this process, and that will continue. Any path forward will preserve the USOPC's mission, governance, leadership and commitment to Team USA athletes.

"This is a moment of real momentum for Team USA. With LA28 and Utah 2034 on home soil, and Team USA's commercial rights returning to the USOPC after the LA28 Games, we're building the capabilities to better grow and support the movement for generations ahead."

Asked if it is open to investment from private equity, institutional capital or sovereign wealth funds, USOPC chief executive Sarah Hirschland told Sportico: "Our responsibility is to look at all of our options, and I would say we are doing that."

The news comes with the world of football bitterly divided over Fifa president Gianni Infantino's failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors, sparking a major backlash.

Asked if the USOPC's bid to seek outside investment would be more successful, Hirschland said: "Our support for Team USA athletes and our national governing bodies is at the centre of our motivation and will remain at the centre of our motivation from start to finish. This is about growing the overall revenue pie for the constituencies that we serve."

Sports.title: Jesus de Miguel death: Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono experiencing 'most difficult days of my life'
Sports.text:
FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.

Tenerife player De Miguel, 30, died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owono during a Spanish second division match on Monday.

The world of football has paid tribute to De Miguel, a father-of-one who joined Tenerife in summer 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all games in European competition this week.

Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on Wednesday, explaining the 25-year-old "wishes to share a few words personally".

"These are the most difficult days of my life," Owono says in the statement.

"I struggle to find the words, and it is very hard for me to come to terms with what has happened.

"I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him.

"I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are all experiencing.

"Rest in peace, Jesus."

Earlier on Wednesday, FC Andorra team-mate Lautaro Spatz defended Owono and said he "would never intentionally hurt anyone" and had been "deeply affected" by De Miguel's death.

Writing on social media, centre-back Spatz said Owono was devastated.

Spatz paid tribute to De Miguel, then said of Owono: "Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone.

"In football, unfortunate incidents can happen but no-one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences."

Players from FC Andorra held a minute's silence before a voluntary training session on Wednesday. Owono was not at the session.

Sports.title: Jesus de Miguel: Canary Islands mourn loss of Tenerife forward
Sports.text:
As you arrive on the holiday island of Tenerife, there is a profound sense of grief, pain and disbelief at the death of footballer Jesus de Miguel.

The Canary island is in mourning for the Tenerife striker, who died from injuries sustained in a collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during a match on Monday.

The 30-year-old had quickly established himself as a club favourite, scoring 11 goals in his first season as Tenerife were promoted to the second tier of Spanish football.

But now the Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez Stadium has become a shrine to the player, with hundreds of people gathering throughout the past few days to lay flowers, light candles and pay their respects.

Bouquets, rosettes sent by clubs from across Spain, prayer cards, photographs, children's drawings and scarves have been laid around the grounds outside gate nine.

It is a deeply moving scene. Fans and residents stand in silence, taking in the tributes.

Many are visibly tearful as the scale of the loss begins to sink in at the very place the incident happened.

Among those paying their respects were Lisa and Lee, visiting Tenerife from Stoke-on-Trent.

They had arrived on holiday at the weekend and decided to attend Monday's match, hoping to experience Spanish football for the first time.

"We never expected something like this to happen," they told BBC Sport.

"We knew it was serious when the players surrounded him [De Miguel], but to see players crying and actually praying on the pitch was very emotional.

"When we found out the news the next day, it just really hit us."

The couple described the atmosphere inside the stadium as sombre and almost completely silent as spectators waited to understand what was happening.

"You always expect somebody to pull through," Lee said. "And then seeing the news the next day, it was just unbelievable."

They returned to the stadium on Wednesday to lay a Port Vale shirt among the tributes, wanting to show their support for the Tenerife community.

"Football has no colours," Lisa said. "If it was one of our players, we'd be heartbroken. They're part of your family."

For Carlos, a player with Tenerife's disability side Tenerife Foundation, the loss is particularly personal.

"Honestly, there are no words to describe him. He was incredible," Carlos said as he lay a flag on the ground.

He described De Miguel as a figure who had helped shape the club's recent history.

"He practically gave his heart and soul for the shirt. He's already a legend at the club because, after all, we were in a very difficult position a few years ago and he helped pull us out of it.

"Without him, I don't think we would be where we are today."

Carlos was at Monday's match and said he was left in shock by what unfolded.

"When I left the stadium I was trembling and I continued to feel that way for hours.

"Right now, we're incredibly hurt and very sad. I also want to send my support to his family, who I can only imagine must be absolutely devastated."

The sense of loss has extended far beyond the stadium.

Poli Suarez, the Canary Islands' minister for education and sport, said Tenerife was in "complete mourning".

"Canarian sport has been left devastated," Suarez told BBC Sport. "The club is broken. Absolutely heartbroken."

Suarez also stressed that the thoughts of everyone were with De Miguel's wife, daughter and wider family.

"They are the ones suffering most directly from this loss, just as the Tenerife supporters are suffering," he said.

The government has pledged its support to the club, players and supporters, with Suarez describing De Miguel as a footballer who had become part of the Canary Islands' sporting history.

"The loss of Jesus de Miguel is now part of our history," Suarez said.

"Not only because of the circumstances of his death, but also because of the affection he always showed towards our island and towards his club."

A further tribute is planned for Saturday at 18:00 GMT, with supporters encouraged to come together to honour his memory.

"It will be an opportunity to show our affection and emotion, and to demonstrate our solidarity with the family," Suarez said.

"We want to show all our affection for Jesus de Miguel."

Sports.title: Man Utd: Michael Carrick run has echoes of Jose Mourinho and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer
Sports.text:
It was impossible not to get swept up in the emotion and delirium of Manchester United's late 3-2 Champions League comeback win against Roma.

Old Trafford was transformed from a mutinous, baying cathedral of distrust and fury to one of joy and celebration.

Nine games and almost eight weeks is an eternity to wait for a victory at a club of Manchester United's size.

It didn't take Michael Carrick long to calm the mood.

"It's one win, so we're not getting too carried away with things, but it was an important win."

It was a huge result in the sense it bought Carrick some time. But given United's general state, no-one can be sure how much.

And, as was quickly pointed out in the aftermath of the victory, Manchester United have been here before.

'Jose Mourinho set to be sacked whatever Manchester United's result vs Newcastle.'

As headlines go, it was attention grabbing.

Saturday, 6 October 2018.

As it turned out, the Mirror was wrong. Although United officials at the time tried to play down the situation, sources have since admitted the intention was to sack Mourinho after presiding over the club's worst start to a season in 29 years, and defeat by Newcastle would make it inevitable.

Much like the Roma game, the visitors raced into a two-goal lead and the atmosphere in the stadium started to turn, with most of the venom aimed at the director's box rather than the manager.

Mourinho, who had promoted Carrick to assistant coach, replaced Eric Bailly with Juan Mata after 19 minutes and it was Mata who scored the 70th-minute goal that sparked the comeback, completed by Alexis Sanchez in the final minute for a 3-2 victory.

After the game, Mourinho said the pressure on him was a "manhunt". However, the relationship between manager and club had been turning sour since the previous summer. His demand for Anthony Martial to be sold had been rejected, while record signing Paul Pogba was proving a problem.

While the Newcastle win sparked an improvement in form, a run of two wins in eight games culminating in a 3-1 loss at Liverpool led to Mourinho's dismissal 10 weeks later.

Former United defender Rio Ferdinand dismissed calls for Ole Gunnar Solskjaer to be sacked before the Champions League encounter with Atalanta on 20 October 2021 as representative of "current fan culture".

Carrick was also part of Solskjaer's coaching group as United went top of the Premier League when they beat Newcastle just over a month earlier, but two wins in seven suggested all was not well.

As he did with Roma, coach Gian Piero Gasperini saw his team establish a two-goal lead by half-time, then collapse. Cristiano Ronaldo was the matchwinner on this occasion, nine minutes from time for another 3-2 win.

Even if United had lost that night, it is hard to think Solskjaer's job would have been under threat. What followed immediately afterwards was a totally different story.

Liverpool came to Old Trafford and established a four-goal first-half lead. Jurgen Klopp's men won 5-0, their biggest ever away win over their old rivals.

Many United fans thought Solskjaer should go that night. It was three weeks later that it happened, after a 4-1 defeat at Watford.

One look at the Premier League table shows why Carrick is right not to get carried away.

If results go against them, Manchester United could be bottom of the table by the time they kick-off against Aston Villa on Sunday.

Neither Mourinho nor Solskjaer could follow up their 3-2 successes with another victory. Mourinho's United drew at Chelsea, then lost at home to Juventus. Solskjaer's United were embarrassed by Liverpool. It meant neither man was able to build on the momentum generated by their epic victories.

That is Carrick's challenge.

United have gone seven Premier League games without a win. They went eight under Ruben Amorim at the end of the 2024-25 campaign, but draws and losses were split by victories en route to the Europa League final, so the effect was not as great as it feels right now.

The club does have an exceptional home record against Villa. They have won their past six in all competitions and lost just two league games against the Midlands outfit at Old Trafford since 1983.

When United sources finally communicated - almost 48 hours after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October - that Carrick and his players would be given the opportunity to turn the situation around, no timescale was put on this. However, the feeling was the forthcoming international break would be an appropriate time for the club hierarchy to take stock and decide what direction they should go in.

In the two games since, Carrick's team have been excellent across two halves.

Victory against Villa, albeit with £70m Carlos Baleba joining the injured list, would haul them up to within two points of Unai Emery's side heading into a tricky run of matches post international break, starting at Liverpool, but also including trips to Newcastle and Arsenal in December. Given he beat Manchester City and Arsenal in his first two games as interim boss.

Defeat is likely to dump them in the relegation zone for at least a fortnight and facing severe baiting at Anfield on 22 November.

"It's not about me," is a phrase Carrick has repeated often as he has assessed the wreckage of another bad result. The outcome against Roma was much more positive.

There is no suggestion Carrick's future has been decided just yet. What happens at Old Trafford this weekend looks very important.

Sports.title: Alexander Zverev 'annoyed' by reaction to him becoming world number one
Sports.text:
Alexander Zverev says he has been "annoyed" by the reaction to him becoming world number one.

The German, 29, claims he is the only tennis player who "has to explain why it's OK" for him to be top of the rankings.

Zverev lost to Italy's Lorenzo Musetti at the Paris Masters on Wednesday - his first match since becoming the ATP Tour's number one for the first time.

He has won his first two Grand Slams titles in 2026, but his success has come in a year in which Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner have struggled with injuries.

"I don't think anybody had to explain themselves as much as I had to do in the last couple of days, which for me, is annoying, to be honest," Zverev said.

Zverev has a 62-8 win-loss record against opponents ranked 11 and below in the world this year - but he has only won three of 12 matches against top-10 players.

Before this year's French Open, Sinner and Alcaraz had shared the past nine Grand Slam titles, with Sinner beating Zverev in last year's Australian Open final.

Zverev has lost in each of his 10 most recent meetings with Sinner, who has not played since Wimbledon after injuring his knee and has subsequently dropped to number two in the rankings.

He has also lost four of his past five matches against Alcaraz, who missed large parts of the season with a wrist injury.

"I was a bit annoyed, to be honest, because achieving the world number one status is something that every player dreams of," said Zverev, who won this year's French Open and US Open titles and lost to Sinner in the final of Wimbledon.

"But then I feel like I'm the only world number in tennis history that has to explain why it's OK for me to be world number one, which I find quite difficult, because I think I deserve to be where I am, even though I lost today."

Zverev did not specify which issues had been annoying him after going to the top of the rankings.

His ascent has led to previous accusations of physical abuse by two of his former partners being highlighted again.

Zverev has always firmly maintained his innocence and has insisted the allegations are baseless.

He was presented with the world number one trophy in Paris on Monday but, after receiving a bye through the first round, was beaten 7-6 (7-5) 6-2 by Musetti.

Looking at his performance on Wednesday, Zverev said: "To simplify it, he played really good and I played really bad.

"I think this was not a very good match from me, I think it might be one of the worst in the last couple of months."

Sports.title: How landmark Everton compensation prevented Burnley record loss
Sports.text:
Six years ago, Burnley were considered one of the best-run clubs in the country.

The Clarets were debt free, with £41.65m cash in the bank, and enjoying their fifth successive season of Premier League football.

Now they sit in the Championship relegation zone, with concerns over debt and the way the Clarets were bought by ALK Capital using loans and the club's own money.

Fans have been very concerned about what the future holds - although on Wednesday there was some rare positive news in the club's accounts.

BBC Sport takes a closer look at what is going on at Turf Moor.

You may be familiar with the term "leverage buyout" after the Glazer family's purchase of Manchester United in 2005.

It effectively means that a purchase is carried out using debt secured on the club's assets, its own bank balance and other loans, rather than the equity of the buyer.

In Burnley's case, ALK Capital took out a £65m loan secured against the club's assets, such as Turf Moor, and used £37m from the club's own bank balance.

On top of that, Velocity Capital, the holding company, owed Burnley £80.1m - money which was also used to buy the club.

The original £65m loan was partially paid off, but then refinanced and extended to reach £105m in the 2024-25 accounts. Interest rates were as high as 12%.

On top of that were factored debts, when a club mortgages off future transfer instalments for a one-off payment from the bank. Burnley owed £37m at an interest rate of 12.75%.

In total, the football club's borrowings stood at £142.3m, the 10th-highest external debt in English football.

Then came the 2025-26 accounts, published today, which painted a different picture.

Now, back to that leveraged buyout which has been attracting so much criticism from fans.

Last season's accounts contained a big surprise.

Remember Velocity Capital, the holding company that owed Burnley £80.1m for the purchase of the club?

The accounts revealed £77.7m of that has now been paid to the Clarets.

It cleared a large chunk of the debt used to buy the football club and helped to make the latest accounts look healthier.

This was needed because, over the past six years, debts related to the leveraged buyout and associated interest payments had increased.

The £77.7m payment, funded by investment from the ownership group, does not mean all Burnley's financial concerns or debts have been resolved.

The club still reported a loss for 2025-26 of £9m, compared with £24m-£29m in the previous three seasons.

That might seem positive.

But this includes the Velocity Capital payment, money for being in the Premier League - and a landmark compensation payout.

The Clarets have been paid £38.8m by Everton because of the Toffees' profit and sustainability breach in 2021-22, which was found to have impacted Burnley's chances of avoiding relegation that season.

Crucially, however, the payout is subject to an appeal, which is expected to be heard in January.

In the accounts, the board stated that "no provision should be included" for the appeal, the result of which could "range between £Nil and the full value of the award detailed being repayable".

This, the club argues, is because "the outcome of the appeal cannot be reasonably determined or measured".

Without the Everton payment, the loss in the 2025-26 accounts would have been £47.8m rather than £9m - a record loss for the club despite it reporting all-time high revenues of £144.5m for the campaign.

Removing the Everton payment might present a more realistic picture of their finances.

Premier League football has been seen as key to Burnley's finances - but the accounts show even in the top flight things were a struggle financially.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, said: "The underlying features are that the club was still losing effectively more than £1m a week.

"That was despite the benefits of being in the Premier League, and therefore relying on player sales and the Everton settlement to reduce the figures to something more palatable."

The three influxes of money helped reduce the debt, and heavy interest repayments.

The club's debt now stands at £62.9m, more than half what it was in 2024-25.

But remember, Burnley had been debt free before the takeover.

There was further improvement, too.

Bank loans have reduced from £105m to £70.1m.

Burnley had also, in recent seasons, mortgaged off future transfer instalments for a one-off payment from the bank, called 'debt factoring'.

Previously at £37m, they reduced it to £16.1m.

This all looks good, but is still reliant on the payment from Everton. If the Toffees do win their appeal, the picture looks very different.

Added to that, £24.2m of the bank loans is due for repayment in January, with another £21.6m falling next August.

The club is in "negotiations to refinance and increase these facilities", but the accounts note that if an agreement is not reached the owners will require "additional finance to repay the amounts due".

What about next season? It will be a season in the Championship, with much lower revenues and no one-off payment from Everton.

The 2026-27 accounts will include player sales of around £38m and parachute payments of £48m.

On the face of it, the numbers look very encouraging for Burnley.

But the accounts laid out that a number of events, including "the outcome of the ongoing compensation ruling appeal", could continue to "cast significant doubt" on the club as a going concern.

Maguire added: "A more forensic look suggests that the underlying issues at Burnley still exist.

"Given that they were in receipt of Premier League broadcast revenues and the benefits of being in the top division, that does suggest that the club faces ongoing challenges.⁠​⁠‍⁠"

On the field, Burnley need a revival - and fast.

It is still early in the Championship season - 14 games have been played - but Burnley sit in the relegation zone.

Over the past six years, they have been a yo-yo club between the Premier League and the Championship, trading the riches of the top flight with strong revenues from a promotion campaign each season.

A big turnaround is needed for that to still be the case under the new management of Swiss Fabio Celestini, who is yet to win in his two games in charge.

Burnley have recorded just one victory in the opening 14 Championship games, leaving them four points adrift in the bottom three.

Recently they set a new English league record for the longest run without a home win, which will reach 400 days when arch-rivals Blackburn visit Turf Moor on 22 November.

Relegation looks more likely than promotion at the moment, and Burnley cannot afford to become the third team in successive seasons to do the double drop from the Premier League to League One.

But time will tell whether the improved results in the accounts start to be replicated on the pitch.

Sports.title: JJ Gabriel transfer news: Real Madrid confident of signing Manchester United forward
Sports.text:
Real Madrid are confident of winning the race to sign Manchester United forward JJ Gabriel after reaching a verbal agreement with the teenager.

The 16-year-old is registered at United, but has not been back to the club since walking out in September.

Gabriel, who played against Atletico Madrid on United's pre-season tour, had been expected to become the club's youngest debutant in September's Carabao Cup tie against Brighton.

However, he has opted to look elsewhere for senior football and has been training on his own in Spain.

His availability alerted clubs around Europe, including Barcelona and Paris St-Germain, but Real now expect to sign the youngster in January.

Though no club-to-club talks have been held, sources have told BBC Sport Real have verbally agreed a deal with Gabriel and his representatives.

Gabriel, who scored a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut, has secured a European Union passport, which is expected to make it easier for him to sign for a club outside England.

United would be due compensation should Gabriel leave, although the figure will be lower if he signs for a club outside the Premier League.

He was named the Premier League's Under-18 player of the season last term, despite being only 14 when the season campaign.

"The best 15-year-old in Europe," was how Gabriel was described by a United source this year, while former interim manager Darren Fletcher said: "The world is his oyster."

Speaking after the EFL Cup defeat by Brighton, United head coach Michael Carrick said: "We've got to be really careful of the whole situation.

"He's a young boy...from a club point of view, looking after our younger players - their welfare, their well-being, their exposure - we've got to be really conscious of that in this situation."

Sports.title: Novak Djokovic: Serb's season over as defeat in Paris means he will miss ATP Finals
Sports.text:
Novak Djokovic is out of the race to qualify for the ATP Finals in Turin after a second-round defeat by qualifier Rinky Hijikata at the Paris Masters.

It means Djokovic, 39, has failed to qualify for the event for only the second time in the past 20 seasons when fit.

The Serb likely needed to reach the semi-finals in Paris to qualify, although the draw had appeared to open up for him after two of his rivals for a place fell earlier in the day.

Despite a good start, Djokovic was unable to repel Australian world number 83 Hijikata in a 2-6 6-3 6-3 defeat.

As Hijikata lifted his level at the end of the second set and throughout the decider, Djokovic, who appeared laboured and to be struggling physically, produced a series of errors, bringing an end to his season.

Djokovic said his plan for the next few weeks is "just rest".

"I'm looking forward to it," he added.

"He was switched on, I wasn't serving as well and he was just playing out of his mind, honestly. He was not missing and keeping the ball low and just a terrific performance.

"He played really amazing tennis and it was my fault to let the control of the match go."

Despite reaching the final of the Australian Open and the semi-finals of Wimbledon, Djokovic has not reached the quarter-final in any of this year's Masters 1000 events.

He won the last of his 24 Grand Slam titles at the US Open in 2023.

Qualifying for Turin would have given him a chance to win a record-extending eighth title at the season-ending championships.

Instead, only Americans Taylor Fritz and Tommy Paul remain in contention to take the final two places currently held by Frances Tiafoe and Rafael Jodar.

Djokovic had not failed to qualify when fit since 2017.

Tiafoe's chances were taken out of his hands earlier on Wednesday when he fell to a 6-3 1-6 7-6 (11-9) defeat by Frenchman Quentin Halys.

Australian Alex de Minaur then failed to take advantage as he lost 7-6 (7-2) 6-3 to Argentine Tomas Martin Etcheverry. A run in Paris could have secured De Minaur's qualification.

Elsewhere, world number one Alexander Zverev and fourth seed Daniil Medvedev, both of whom have already qualified for Turin, were also beaten.

Zverev said he was "annoyed" by the response to him becoming world number one after a straight-sets loss to Lorenzo Musetti, while Medvedev was beaten 6-4 6-4 by Peruvian world number 33 Ignacio Buse.

Fritz teetered on the brink of elimination but came through a decisive third-set tie-break to win 6-7 (6-8) 7-5 7-6 (7-5) against 78th-ranked Alex Molcan of Slovakia.

Earlier, Paul beat Spain's Daniel Merida 6-1 6-1.

Sports.title: Jodie Burrage receives WTA support after social media abuse following Chennai Open defeat
Sports.text:
Britain's Jodie Burrage has been receiving support from WTA staff at an event in India after being sent death threats on social media.

Burrage, 27, was bombarded with abusive online messages when she was beaten in her first WTA Tour singles main-draw match in 16 months on Tuesday.

On Wednesday, she won in the last 16 of the Chennai Open doubles alongside Robin Montgomery of the United States.

"Protecting players and the wider tennis family from online threats and abuse is a key priority for the WTA," the governing body told BBC Sport.

"We have WTA staff on the ground in Chennai offering Jodie support, along with our wider player welfare and Threat Matrix team."

Burrage shared a story on her Instagram account that showed the direct messages she had been sent following a 3-6 6-3 7-5 loss to India's Vaishnavi Adkar.

"Nice welcome back to tour. I remember why I left," Burrage wrote.

Burrage tagged the WTA into the post, asking when action will be taken to combat abuse. Other players, including Germany's Eva Lys, showed solidarity with the former world number 85.

The WTA insists it is taking a "proactive approach" to protecting female players from abuse.

The Threat Matrix system, which uses artificial intelligence-led detection, can identify people behind the accounts that threaten players, enabling investigations to take place and potentially leading to legal action.

Female players were subjected to more than 12,000 abusive posts and messages on social media last year, according to data from the service.

"Through Threat Matrix, a system we established in 2023, delivered by Signify Group alongside World Tennis, we identify, investigate and take action against those responsible," the WTA added.

"This includes reporting abusive content for removal, escalating serious cases to law enforcement and supporting action to prevent real-world harm.

"As much of the abuse players receive comes through direct messages, the WTA has offered Jodie additional support.

"These include a private channel to report abusive direct messages, and moderation that hides abusive comments on public channels before she sees them."

In 2024, a report from Signify found that angry gamblers were behind 48% of posts which were deemed to be abusive.

They were responsible for 42% of verified abuse in 2025 and 59% of cases of serious abuse.

The WTA is working with several gambling companies in a programme that flags abuse from gamblers in real time, allowing the operator to take direct action against those targeting athletes.

The company is then able to flag, restrict or suspend the account.

Mhairi Maclennan, chief executive of the Kyniska Advocacy, which supports female athletes, believes there is "still not enough being done" to protect athletes across the board.

"I'm afraid it is all too common for athletes who have public profiles to receive this type of abuse," she told BBC Radio 5 Live's Drive programme.

"Whether they have won or lost, a lot of the athletes we speak to report they have received abuse - whether death threats or rape threats - because of their public profile and because sports like tennis are tied to betting.

"Sports need a healthier relationship with betting agencies. Ultimately sports need money but we need to be looking at what betting is doing to individual athletes and looking after their welfare."

Sports.title: Esteban Ocon dropped – is it the end of his F1 career?
Sports.text:
Esteban Ocon's career as a Formula 1 race driver is over - at least for the foreseeable future - after a falling-out with Haas led to the Frenchman being dropped for the rest of this season.

Ocon, 30, was already going to be leaving Haas at the end of the year, with little prospect of finding a seat on the grid next season.

But the acrimonious turn of events in Mexico City last weekend brought that forward by a few races.

Ocon now faces a year on the sidelines, with the aim of finding a berth as a reserve driver, as he seeks to rebuild his career.

This is not the first time he has found himself in this situation.

Ocon was also without a seat in 2019 when he lost his drive at what had been called the Force India team after it was bought by Canadian billionaire Lawrence Stroll, who put his son Lance in Ocon's car.

This, though, feels like it has more potential finality about it. Not least because, 10 years into his career in F1, Ocon is well known within the sport for both his competitive level and his approach.

He's been around the block a few times. His career has not been especially stellar. He has a reputation for falling out with teams and team-mates. And there is a new generation breaking through in F1, led by new world champion Kimi Antonelli.

The catalyst for Ocon's departure from Haas was a falling-out with team principal Ayao Komatsu after Friday practice in Mexico City last weekend.

Exactly what led to him being dropped is unknown. No-one is talking, not even off the record, and lawyers are now involved.

What is known is that Ocon objected over the team radio while in the car to being told by his engineer Laura Mueller that they were switching his run plan from using soft tyres for his race-simulation run to mediums.

Ocon said to Mueller: "No, no. I wanted the soft. Don't do that to me. Come on."

It seems the argument carried on after the session with Komatsu. The announcement that he was dropped for the weekend came on Saturday morning.

Later that day, Ocon put out a statement on social media admitting "a difference in viewpoints led to a discussion with the parties involved" but adding that he "categorically rejected any reports or allegations suggesting that any form of physical violence was used to resolve any differences of any nature".

That followed a report in France's L'Equipe newspaper saying a meeting between Komatsu and Ocon "ended abruptly, perhaps even physically".

Haas said nothing more over the weekend in Mexico but on Tuesday evening put out what was already being seen as the inevitable announcement that he would not drive for the team again.

Haas had already run out of patience with Ocon long before Mexico City but whatever happened there was serious enough that Komatsu felt the relationship had to end on the spot.

The decline of Ocon's time with Haas has echoes of previous experiences.

Ocon has been beaten by team-mate Oliver Bearman over his two seasons at Haas, just as he was outpaced by Pierre Gasly and before him Fernando Alonso at Alpine, and Daniel Ricciardo before that when the team was known as Renault.

When Haas signed Ocon, his reputation was such that many were surprised they had taken him. Komatsu felt he could make it work.

But the team began to notice a pattern. When Ocon was struggling, he would become defensive and blame the team and car. Tensions would rise and the team felt there was a lack of accountability from the driver.

There were also clashes with his team-mate, for example in Monaco practice when they got in each other's way and Bearman ended up calling Ocon "an idiot" over the radio.

They also crashed into each other towards the end of the British Grand Prix last year.

Competitive tensions between team-mates are common in F1. A driver's team-mate is also their biggest rival - the only person with the same equipment so the only driver against which they can be directly measured.

The parallel need to work together to benefit the team's overall prospects can be an uncomfortable ask in such circumstances.

It's a problem that is causing tension at Ferrari between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, for example, as was also seen in Mexico.

But over the years, Ocon has built an unenviable reputation for both these sides of his character. To outsiders, this can be surprising because he is charm personified with the media, a delight to deal with.

He and Gasly - who were childhood friends before falling out nearly 20 years ago - crashed twice together at Alpine. The end of their two seasons together was the first occasion on which Ocon was released before the end of the season, dropped with one race to go.

Alonso and Ocon also fell out and the Spanish icon did not trouble to hide his distaste for his team-mate's behaviour at times. Ocon also had on-track clashes and team radio disputes with Sergio Perez when at Force India.

Alpine also saw the same pattern as did Haas more recently in terms of self-awareness and accountability.

Alonso put in a starring performance in wet qualifying in Canada in 2022 and stuck his midfield Alpine on the front row alongside Max Verstappen's Red Bull.

That lap was 1.6 seconds faster than Ocon's and team insiders say he simply could not accept that he had been that much slower.

Ocon is said to have insisted there must have been something wrong with his car and continued to do so for several races. The team checked and checked and there was nothing wrong. It was just Alonso doing what great drivers sometimes do and redefining perceptions of what was possible.

All drivers complain. It's part of their make-up. Their motivation comes from believing they can be the best, and finding weaknesses in the car and improving them is their job and how they make themselves and the team more competitive.

The better they are, the more acceptable that complaining is. Verstappen, for example, is constantly having a go about clunky gearshifts or a balance he does not like. Red Bull accept it because he delivers on track at such a high level on such a consistent basis.

Ocon's issue is that there is a different pattern. On average, he has been slower than Bearman these last two years, just as he was against Gasly from 2023-24, against Alonso from '21-22 and against Ricciardo in 2020.

Ocon is managed by Mercedes and came through their young driver programme.

When he lost his Force India seat, it was Mercedes that took him on as reserve driver in 2019.

At one point, team principal Toto Wolff was considering putting Ocon in the race team alongside Hamilton. One of the reasons he did not was he thought their characters would clash, that the relationship would be too combustible. Valtteri Bottas was retained for 2020 after all.

At the same time, George Russell, the next Mercedes protege, was excelling for Williams, and Mercedes concluded from the data they had on both that Russell was their guy for the future, not Ocon.

That was effectively the end of Ocon's career as a potential candidate for a top team but Mercedes helped him back on to the grid with a drive at Renault in 2020, before the team was rebranded Alpine in 2021.

It was for them that Ocon took his sole victory, at the 2021 Hungarian Grand Prix. He drove well but the win owed a substantial amount to fortune.

The start was wet and there was a multi-car pile-up that took out Bottas and both Red Bulls.

Ocon came out of that pile-up running second to Hamilton. The race was red-flagged. By the time it was restarted, the track was drying.

At the end of the formation lap, every single car pitted for dry-weather slick tyres bar Hamilton, who took to the grid on his own.

He had to stop on the next lap, falling to the back. That put Ocon into the lead from Sebastian Vettel's Aston Martin, a car of similar performance on a track where overtaking is difficult. Ocon and Alpine managed the race well to stay in front of the four-time champion throughout.

Hamilton spent the rest of the race fighting back and his pace was so superior it appeared he might win.

Until he caught Alonso, that is. The Spaniard, who had been delayed by rather than benefitting from the first-lap crash, was running fourth, close behind Ocon, Vettel and Carlos Sainz's Ferrari.

Alonso knew what was at stake, that if Hamilton passed him quickly, the Briton would almost certainly win the race. And he knew what a win would mean for Alpine.

The team's last victory had been in 2013 but that was when they were known as Lotus and were under different owners. Renault's most recent win had been secured by Alonso - at the 2008 Japanese Grand Prix.

Alonso won his two world titles for Renault. He had been brought back to F1 after a two-year break by Renault. And so he fought as hard as he knew to keep Hamilton at bay for as long as possible.

The Mercedes was so much faster that at times it looked as if Hamilton might drive through or over Alonso. Instead, using all his skill and guile, he held Hamilton back for 10 laps.

When Hamilton finally passed Alonso, there were only five laps to go. Within two, he was past Sainz but he did not have time to make any further progress before the chequered flag.

Ocon and Alonso celebrated together with the team after the win.

Yet little more than a year later, relations had deteriorated to the point that, after a clash between the pair at the Brazilian Grand Prix at the end of 2022, shortly before Alonso was leaving the team to move to Aston Martin, the two-time champion sarcastically referred to Ocon as "our friend" over the radio.

Out of the car, asked whether he would speak to Ocon about the incident, he said: "I don't need to. One more race. Then it's over, finally."

For Ocon, it's now over at Haas, too. Finding a way back on to the grid won't be easy.
Sports.description: Esteban Ocon's career as a Formula 1 race driver is over - at least for the foreseeable future - after a falling-out with Haas led to the Frenchman being dropped for the rest of this season. Ocon, 30, was already going to be leaving Haas at the end of the year, with little prospect of finding a seat on the grid...

Sports.title: Could Hyrox's Olympic ambition spell the end for triathlon?
Sports.text:
"Our biggest concern is that they're not just here to take part, they're here to take over."

British triathlete Max Stapley first saw the news on Instagram. Last week, World Triathlon announced it was partnering with Hyrox - the fitness craze which combines running with exercise stations.

The agreement means Hyrox becomes a recognised discipline within World Triathlon. And now it sits under a recognised international federation, it could be eligible for inclusion at the Olympics and Paralympics.

It is too late for the Los Angeles 2028 Games but is there room for both hybrid racing and triathlon to feature at a future Olympics? Or could one replace the other?

For triathlon, a sport which has been in the Olympics since 2000, and has long-established professional circuits, its athletes are questioning whether they'll reap any rewards from this partnership - or even, whether it could "kill" the sport altogether.

Stapley, who spoke to BBC Sport from a training camp in Thailand, was having dinner with friends when his phone started pinging with news of the proposals and reaction to them.

"I was like, hold on a minute, what's this?", said Stapley.

"We don't even get an early notification, we found out on Instagram".

The post read, external: 'Hyrox x World Triathlon are officially introducing 'Hybrid Racing' as a new discipline within the World Triathlon family.'

Sophie Evans - who won gold as part of England's Commonwealth Games mixed relay team in Birmingham in 2022 - said she was "surprised" to receive the news like that.

"I'm not actually against it being part of World Triathlon. It's more the fact we were blindsided, it's just like it's here," she added.

Stapley accused World Triathlon of not caring about its athletes because he did not receive any communication from his sport's governing body prior to and after the announcement was made.

"They have no respect for us," he said. "They don't even contact us like 'hey, do you guys actually care about this, or what do you think?'"

In response, a World Triathlon spokesperson told BBC Sport: "The World Triathlon Executive Board approved the partnership. The board includes representatives of the World Triathlon Athletes' Committee elected by their peers.

"Athlete representatives are involved in every executive board discussion, and their voice is always heard.

"The announcement was communicated through the same procedures followed for all World Triathlon releases."

World Triathlon says the partnership is designed to "benefit the entire World Triathlon movement",, external with new opportunities to engage athletes and audiences, and a stronger platform to grow triathlon and multisport from grassroots to elite level.

The question for athletes is, how?

European champion Roksana Slupek, of Poland, said she was "not against the idea", but wanted more information.

"What's the benefit for us, for triathlon? It's nothing against Hyrox," said Slupek.

However, Stapley called the move an "attack on our whole existence" and is concerned that World Triathlon could direct attention and resources towards Hyrox's Olympic ambition - at the expense of his own sport.

"How does Hyrox grow triathlon? If anything they've killed triathlon," he said, while also suggesting brands would rather get in early with Hyrox athletes before they potentially appear at an Olympics.

"Sponsorships have reduced because there's no visibility on TV, you have to pay to watch us.

"We are triathletes that do the short distance, which is the Olympic distance, and we've trained all our lives for it.

"There's no swimming, there's no biking, it's indoors. [Hyrox] has got nothing to do [with triathlon]".

"It seems like our sport's gone, 'no worries, come along, use our structure, use our access to the International Olympic Committee, and perhaps take our space'.

"We've got an opportunity to win medals in Los Angeles [at the 2028 Olympics], but will we have it further down the track?"

Evans said that while triathlon was an "established" Olympic sport, that has provided high quality racing since its introduction to the Games 26 years ago, this new partnership has introduced a "level of uncertainty".

"A lot of the resistance has come from athletes, because you don't know," she added.

A World Triathlon spokesperson told BBC Sport, it is continuing to "increase its focus and involvement in the Olympic and Paralympic families" and that it is in the "planning phase" for Brisbane 2032, adding that "triathlon is, and will remain, at the heart of everything we do".

BBC Sport approached Hyrox for comment, but they referred us to the statements made by World Triathlon.

Sam Dickinson - who won an Olympic triathlon bronze in Paris as part Team GB's relay quartet - can see why the move makes sense but wants more clarity.

"It's trying to get people active not from an elite side but from a participation side," Dickinson told BBC Sport.

"So in that sense it does make sense that as a multi-sport it comes under the World Triathlon umbrella.

"But it's early days, we don't have any of the bread and butter of exactly what's going on."

And there lies the crux of the problem - the lack of clarity has fuelled speculation about what the future holds.

World Triathlon does have other disciplines in its remit, such as Aquathlon and duathlon.

BBC Sport has been told that 'Fitness Racing' was first included as a discipline in the World Triathlon Constitution in October 2025, a move supported by the majority of the governing body's National Federations.

A World Triathlon spokesperson added that the partnership provides opportunities to 'reach new audiences' through collaborating with global partners.

Founded in 2017, Hyrox's popularity has continued to grow rapidly. A total of 1.5m athletes took part during the 2025/26 season - up from 650,000 the year before - with participation projected to surpass 2m in the current season.

British Triathlon, one of World Triathlon's national federations, told BBC Sport it recognises "World Triathlon's work to grow, develop and strengthen the sport of triathlon, multi-sport and its community", but is waiting to hear the "full operational, governance and commercial framework" for the partnership.

Sports.title: England must improve discipline says RFU chief Bill Sweeney
Sports.text:
England must improve their discipline given they are the second-best side in the world when they have 15 players on the pitch, says Rugby Football Union chief executive Bill Sweeney.

During a miserable Six Nations campaign, England received eight yellow cards and one red across five matches, meaning they played 118 minutes - almost a game and a half of rugby - at less than a full complement.

They finished the 45-21 defeat by South Africa in July with 13 men after yellow cards for Tommy Freeman and Guy Pepper, while four second-half sin-binnings contributed to Argentina coming close to a successful fightback a fortnight later.

"It has been a big internal discussion," said Sweeney, who claims analysis also shows England slip to eighth or ninth best in the world when they are down to 14 players.

"[Head coach] Steve [Borthwick]'s very conscious of that and he's working really hard with the players to improve that aspect.

"You need all your players on the pitch for as long as possible. That's something we need to address."

England face Australia on Sunday in the first match of their November campaign.

Borthwick's side comfortably won last autumn's meeting between the two teams, but the Wallabies' shock 42-37 victory in 2024 is a recent reminder of their quality.

After matches against Japan (14 November) and New Zealand (21 November), England will play another southern hemisphere opponent in the first Nations Championship finals weekend at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

The new biennial event, introduced to bring a clearer narrative to the Test calendar outside of Rugby World Cup and British and Irish Lions tour years, culminates in six play-off matches over three days.

The teams at the top of the northern and southern hemisphere standings will play off for the Nations Championship title, while all matches count towards a Ryder Cup-style Hemisphere Shield trophy.

Sweeney admitted ticket sales for Friday's fixtures - which will see the sixth-placed and third-placed teams in their respective standings face off at 16:40 and 20:10 GMT respectively - had been "challenging" as the new tournament attempts to fill an 82,000-seater venue.

The upper tier of Allianz Stadium has yet to be opened, with plenty of seats still available in the lower section.

The identity of the teams involved in Friday's play-offs will only be finalised after the previous weekend's action.

With three of six rounds played, the current standings would pit Italy against Fiji in the day's first game, and England against Australia in its headline fixture.

"It's uncharted waters," Sweeney told BBC Sport of the finals weekend.

"Saturday and Sunday ticket sales are going well - Friday's a challenge at the moment.

"We're waiting to see how things go after this weekend when things start to firm up a bit and you'll get a better idea of where the league rankings are.

"A lot of fans still don't fully understand what it is and we've done a fair bit of education, but maybe not enough.

"Friday does remain a challenge, but we're confident that we'll see an uptick in ticket sales."

Sports.title: World Series champion Teixeira wins US House seat as former NFL reporter Tafoya’s Senate bid fails
Sports.text:
Former World Series champion turned Republican politician Mark Teixeira will represent ⁠Texas’s 21st congressional district in Washington after defeating Democrat Kristin Hook in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

On Wednesday morning, Teixeira was leading with 54.5% ⁠of the ​votes after 99% of the ballots had been counted.

“Tonight’s victory belongs ⁠to the people of Texas’s 21st District. I’m not going to Washington for myself, but rather to be a strong, responsive ⁠voice for every family in this district,” wrote on X. “Together, we can build a ​better future for our families, ‌our neighbors, and every community ‌across Texas 21. I’m excited to get to work. I will ‌be praying for all of you and for the future of this great nation. God bless Texas, and God bless America.“

Teixeira’s victory was expected. The seat has been in Republican hands since 1979. It was previously held by Chip Roy, who didn’t run for reelection. The district includes deeply conservative parts of Texas in the Austin ‌and San Antonio areas.

Donald Trump and Texas’s Republican governor, Greg Abbott, endorsed Teixeira’s campaign. Abbott lost his ​reelection campaign against Democrat Gina Hinojosa, and the Republicans suffered sweeping losses across the US in a repudiation of Trump’s second term in power.

According to Teixeira’s campaign website he aims to “end radical woke indoctrination, defend parental rights, kill DEI, restore patriotic education rooted in American and Texas values … and fight against Cultural Marxism.”

Teixeira, 46, was born and raised in Maryland, and he attended Georgia Tech. A first-round draft pick by the Rangers in 2001, he played for Texas ⁠from 2003-07 before stints with the Atlanta Braves (2007-08), Los Angeles Angels (2008) ​and New York ​Yankees (2009-16). Teixeira was selected an All-Star ​in 2005, 2009 and 2015, and he helped the Yankees ​win the 2009 ‌World Series. ​

The race that secured Democratic control of the Senate also featured a decorated athlete. Josh Turek, a four-time US Paralympian and double wheelchair basketball gold medallist, flipped a Republican-held seat in Iowa, with his victory putting the Democrats over the line at about 11.25pm US Eastern Time by guaranteeing them at least 51 seats.

Turek, 47, was born with spina bifida and underwent 21 operations before his 13th birthday. He won bronze at London 2012 and gold at Rio 2016 and Tokyo 2020 before winning election to the Iowa House of Representatives in 2022.

Elsewhere in the midterms, former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, who was running as a Republican, lost her bid for the US Senate in Minnesota to Peggy Flanagan, the state’s Democratic lieutenant governor. Tafoya did not actively seek out support from Trump and broke ranks with Republicans over the war with Iran. She also portrayed herself as pro choice but did not clarify her exact stance on access to abortion.

Minnesota has not elected a Republican to the US Senate since 2002. Flanagan is also the first Native American woman to be elected to the upper chamber.

In Alabama, former college football coach Tommy Tuberville, a Republican, won the race to become Alabama governor. The 72-year-old formerly coached Auburn, one of the most popular college teams in Alabama.

Gaming_Tech.title: Canva announces major job cuts after 'our hardest year yet'
Gaming_Tech.text:
Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.

In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.

The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms.

It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff.

The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said.

"For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today."

The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.

Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn.

Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products.

"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.

Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.

The company offers a variety of templates and tools to help users without technical skills or a design background to create a range of professional-looking graphics and presentations, from wedding invitations to business pitch decks.

Gaming_Tech.title: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
Gaming_Tech.text:
French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.

The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies.

"No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.

Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.

Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.

Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.

But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.

While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.

Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.

Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.

In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers.

By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.

According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted.

"The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.

The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.

But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them.

"Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.

Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.

It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.

Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe.

"We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens.

"Even pots in Ukraine were left alone."
